## Why This Is Asked

## Key Concepts

- Idempotence achieved through stateful module parameters (e.g., `state: present`)
- Check mode (`--check`) for safe dry-run validation
- Dynamic inventory and conditional tasks for multi-OS compatibility

## Code Example
```yaml
# inventory/hosts.yml
all:
  hosts:
    web1:
      ansible_host: 10.0.0.1
    web2:
      ansible_host: 10.0.0.2
  children:
    debian:
      hosts:
        web1:
        web2:
    rhel:
      hosts:
        web3:
        web4:
        web5:
```

```yaml
# site.yml
- hosts: all
  become: true
  roles:
    - web
```

```yaml
# roles/web/tasks/main.yml
- name: Install Nginx (Debian)
  ansible.builtin.apt:
    name: nginx
    state: present
  when: ansible_facts.os_family == "Debian"

- name: Install Nginx (RHEL)
  ansible.builtin.yum:
    name: nginx
    state: present
  when: ansible_facts.os_family == "RedHat"

- name: Deploy static site
  ansible.builtin.template:
    src: index.html.j2
    dest: /var/www/html/index.html
    mode: '0644'

- name: Configure Nginx site
  ansible.builtin.copy:
    dest: /etc/nginx/sites-available/static
    content: |
      server {
        listen 80;
        server_name _;
        root /var/www/html;
        index index.html;
      }
  notify: Reload Nginx

- name: Enable site
  ansible.builtin.file:
    src: /etc/nginx/sites-available/static
    dest: /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/static
    state: link
  notify: Reload Nginx

- name: Allow HTTP/HTTPS (Debian)
  community.general.ufw:
    rule: allow
    port: '{{ item }}'
    proto: tcp
  loop: [80, 443]
  when: ansible_facts.os_family == "Debian"

- name: Allow HTTP/HTTPS (RHEL)
  ansible.posix.firewalld:
    service: '{{ item }}'
    permanent: true
    immediate: true
    state: enabled
  loop: [http, https]
  when: ansible_facts.os_family == "RedHat"

- name: Start/enable Nginx
  ansible.builtin.service:
    name: nginx
    state: started
    enabled: true
```

```yaml
# roles/web/handlers/main.yml
- name: Reload Nginx
  ansible.builtin.service:
    name: nginx
    state: reloaded
```

questions.explanation: There are several Kubernetes mechanisms that work together to ensure proper pod scheduling and resource reservation. First, you can use nodeSelector with node labels to constrain pods to specific nodes. For example, label a node with `kubectl label nodes node-name dedicated=high-priority`, then add `nodeSelector` to your pod spec. Second, to prevent other pods from using those reserved nodes, apply taints to the nodes with `kubectl taint nodes node-name dedicated=high-priority:NoSchedule`, then add corresponding tolerations to the pods that should be allowed to run on them. Third, use PodPriority and preemption so that when cluster resources are constrained, the scheduler will evict lower-priority pods to make room for critical workloads. Create a PriorityClass with a high value (e.g., 1000000) and assign it to critical pods. Real-world example: In a production cluster, you might taint three nodes as 'performance-critical:NoSchedule' and have a PriorityClass of 'critical-system' with value 1000000, then deploy your database and API pods with these settings to ensure they always have dedicated resources. This prevents noisy neighbor issues where less critical workloads starve critical services of CPU or memory.

questions.explanation:
Pod Disruption Budgets (PDBs) are Kubernetes objects that specify the minimum number or percentage of pods that must remain running during voluntary disruptions. When an administrator initiates a node drain or a rolling update occurs, the scheduler checks the PDB constraints before evicting pods. If evicting a pod would violate the PDB, the disruption is blocked until sufficient pods are healthy to maintain the specified availability threshold.

The scheduler integrates with PDBs through the disruption controller, which evaluates whether pod eviction is safe. For example, a deployment with 6 replicas and a PDB requiring 4 available pods ensures that no more than 2 pods can be disrupted simultaneously. Key strategies to prevent downtime include setting appropriate PDB thresholds (typically 50-80% availability), implementing health checks and readiness probes, using progressive deployment strategies like rolling updates with proper surge settings, and maintaining buffer capacity in cluster resources to allow for graceful pod replacements during maintenance windows.

questions.explanation:
A Dockerfile is a declarative text document that automates Docker image creation through a series of instructions:

• **Base Image**: Starts with a foundation OS or runtime using `FROM`
• **Environment Setup**: Configures working directories, environment variables, and system dependencies
• **Application Code**: Copies source files and installs application-specific dependencies
• **Runtime Configuration**: Exposes ports and defines the default command to execute
• **Layer Caching**: Each instruction creates a new layer, enabling efficient builds and updates
• **Reproducibility**: Ensures consistent environments across development, testing, and production

**Common Dockerfile Instructions:**
```dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine          # Base image
WORKDIR /usr/src/app         # Set working directory
COPY package*.json ./        # Copy dependency files
RUN npm ci --only=production # Install dependencies
COPY . .                     # Copy application code
EXPOSE 3000                  # Document port usage
USER node                    # Run as non-root user
CMD ["npm", "start"]         # Default command
```

**Best Practices:**
• Use multi-stage builds to reduce image size
• Leverage .dockerignore to exclude unnecessary files
• Run containers as non-root users for security
• Minimize layers by combining RUN commands
• Use specific base image tags for consistency

questions.explanation: The solution involves two key Kubernetes scheduling mechanisms working together. First, apply taints to GPU nodes using `kubectl taint nodes <node-name> nvidia.com/gpu=present:NoSchedule` - this prevents any pods without the matching toleration from being scheduled on those nodes. Then, add a toleration to GPU workload pods that explicitly requires the GPU resource: `tolerations: - key: 'nvidia.com/gpu' operator: 'Exists' effect: 'NoSchedule'`. For additional control, you can use node affinity to prefer GPU nodes for workloads that can run there: `nodeAffinity: preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution: - weight: 100 preference: matchExpressions: - key: 'nvidia.com/gpu' operator: 'Exists'`. A common real-world pattern is to also add labels to GPU nodes (e.g., `node-role.kubernetes.io/gpu=true`) for more flexible matching. This approach ensures proper isolation while maintaining flexibility - GPU pods can be specifically targeted to GPU nodes, and non-GPU pods are automatically excluded due to the taint. This is essential in production environments where GPU resources are expensive and limited, such as ML inference workloads at companies like Netflix, Spotify, or Airbnb.

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

This question evaluates practical GitOps competencies: multi-environment repo structuring, canary deployment implementation with Argo Rollouts, drift detection and self-healing, and comparative knowledge of Flux. It also assesses understanding of declarative configuration, promotion workflows, and Git as the single source of truth.

## Key Concepts

- **App of Apps Pattern**: Hierarchical application management in ArgoCD, where a root Application orchestrates child Applications for each environment
- **Argo Rollouts Canary**: Traffic splitting, metric analysis, and automated progression/rollback decisions
- **App Reconciliation**: Continuous sync ensures cluster state matches Git; drift is auto-repaired
- **Git as Source of Truth**: All desired state is version-controlled; clusters auto-heal to match
- **Secrets Management**: Integrate external secrets operators (ESO, Sealed Secrets) to manage sensitive data safely in GitOps workflows

## Code Example

```yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata:
  name: my-app-canary
  namespace: staging
spec:
  replicas: 4
  strategy:
    canary:
      trafficRouting:
        istio:
          virtualService:
            name: my-app-vs
            routes:
              - primary
      steps:
        - setWeight: 10
        - pause: { duration: 5m }
        - analysis:
            templates:
              - templateName: success-rate
            args:
              - name: service-name
                value: my-app-staging
      canaryMetadata:
        labels:
          track: canary
      stableMetadata:
        labels:
```

## Interview Context
This question tests understanding of GitOps principles and ArgoCD's role in modern DevOps workflows. Interviewers want to assess your knowledge of deployment automation, Git repository management, and Kubernetes ecosystem tools.

- **GitOps Principles**: Git as single source of truth, declarative configurations, automated synchronization

```yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: webapp
  namespace: argocd
spec:
```

questions.explanation:
Pod affinity and anti-affinity rules control pod placement relative to other pods. For high availability across availability zones, you would use topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone with anti-affinity rules. A common pattern is to set podAntiAffinity to distribute replicas across zones (using 'Required' for strict enforcement), while using podAffinity to co-locate related services like a frontend with its cache or sidecar proxies on the same node.

For example, a 3-replica StatefulSet would use podAntiAffinity with topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname (or topology.kubernetes.io/zone for zone-level distribution) to ensure each replica lands on a different node/zone. The matchExpressions allow targeting pods by label selectors. You can combine both - anti-affinity for the application pods across zones, and affinity to keep logging sidecars co-located with the main container.

The difference between requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution and preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution is critical: required rules must be satisfied or the pod won't schedule (useful for zone distribution), while preferred rules are best-effort and allow scheduling even if the preference can't be met (useful when you want balanced distribution but can tolerate some imbalance).

questions.explanation: Taints and tolerations work together to control pod scheduling—nodes repel pods unless they have matching tolerations. To dedicate GPU nodes, apply taints to nodes with GPU hardware (e.g., `kubectl taint nodes gpu-node gpu=present:NoSchedule`), then add tolerations to GPU workloads (e.g., `tolerations: - key: gpu operator: Equal value: present effect: NoSchedule`). For critical monitoring pods that must run on all nodes, use tolerations with `operator: Exists` and `effect: NoExecute` to tolerate any taint, or specify `tolerationSeconds` to control auto-eviction timing. The scheduler evaluates pod tolerations against node taints to determine valid placement, ensuring GPU workloads only run on GPU-equipped nodes while critical pods can be scheduled anywhere.
